COVID: The Standoff - Virus vs Townships

By: Ntokozo Miya | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Accused of not taking the Covid-19 pandemic seriously, residents in townships and informal settlements say they are doing the best they can with the little they have.

Unique Selling Point:
Following the first confirmed case of Covid-19 in Alexandra, we speak to residents and organisations who say they are putting up a good fight but might lose due to population density in the area. We spend a day with Linda Twala, a beloved businessman and philanthropist in Alexandra who is known for being hands-on in his community outreach programs. We go from his charity storeroom where food parcels are prepared for distribution among the needy and elderly in Alexandra, and we see him making deliveries and interact with beneficiaries. We also get to interview the beneficiaries about what they are doing to protect themselves from the virus.

Summary:
The challenges in informal settlements are well-known but organisations and individuals are making a difference despite huge and valid concerns about population density. We focus on efforts to contain the spread in Alexandra seeing as it is the most densely populated township in Johannesburg and has most recently confirmed its first case. The organisations we speak to seek to address the two biggest concerns where the virus is concerned in townships – washing hands and people having enough food to minimise the need to go out and potentially expose themselves and others to the virus. Our focus takes a national approach as we use social media videos from other provinces including the Eastern Cape and an interview with Social Juctice Coalition to give an overview of the sanitation challenges associated with densely populated communities across the country. For the KZN perspective, we have a freelance producer and cameraman who is familiar with townships around the Durban area and will be able to take us into an informal settlement home of a family living a small shack and interview them about their water and sanitation challenges as well as the difficulty in maintaining social distancing. They will also tell us if KZN government interventions have filtered to them and if they have been able to access social welfare assistance. We will use a graphic to separate the stories from each province so that they do not pile on top of each other.

Further information:
We also cover Soweto where Salaamedia, an organisation of humanitarian journalists, started collecting soap donations as soon as news of the virus spread under the tag #SoapBarCampaign. Their beneficiaries are mainly homes for the disadvantaged in Soweto where many people share dorms and dining halls. Part of their #CoronaSoldiers campaign has been to educate their beneficiaries about the virus because it was apparent that information had not really filtered to people on the ground – many still don't understand how the virus affects the body and exactly why the lockdown is necessary. They also run a Facebook Live station with over 21 000 followers where they try to reach people on social media and give them up-to-date and accurate information on the virus.

Among their priorities right now is sourcing face masks for health professionals as a response to widespread calls to protect the very healthcare workers who service generally underprivileged communities.

Script:


THE STANDOFF – TOWNSHIPS VS COVID-19 – FOR FINAL MIX
ELONA – ALEXANDRA RESIDENT
One toilet, one hundred people. We have to jump the street to get to the toilet.
THENJISWA QEDA – LAMONTVILLE RESIDENT
Sixteen of us live in this container.
ABONGILE BULO – KHAYELITSHA RESIDENT
We don't have water to wash hands and prevent the coronavirus. Maybe we will be infected.
VO – From Gauteng to the Western Cape, millions of South Africans living in townships and informal settlements were plunged into despair when the government announced the national lockdown in March --- a desperate move to slow the spread of the deadly coronavirus.
High on the agenda was to prevent an outbreak in these communities but confined to small living quarters and with limited food and water, and no means to earn an income for weeks on end - how would the country's most vulnerable survive?
LINK – In densely populated townships and informal settlements where social distancing is near impossible, government's lockdown strategy to counter the Coronavirus pandemic has been put to the test.
GAUTENG
VO – Now three weeks into the lockdown that has since been extended, it’s clear that these communities are taking strain.
Gauteng is geographically the smallest province but with 15 million residents, many of whom live in informal settlements, it faces the biggest challenge.
By Thursday, nine hundred and sixty nine cases of Covid-19 infections were recorded within its borders - the most in the country, cementing its place as the red zone.
MPHIKISENI XIMBA – ALEXANDRA RESIDENT
We are overcrowded because there are no houses.
VO – Alexandra township's Mphikiseni Ximba survives on a social grant in this two-room house with his family of eleven. They live in a yard with six other families, with whom they share one tap and one toilet.
He says he has been vigilant about teaching his children the importance of using the sanitizer given to him by a local NGO.
MPHIKISENI XIMBA – ALEXANDRA RESIDENT
Even this one, you can see he's very young but he knows what to do. There's a bottle hanging on the wall, he goes there and also sanitises his hands.
VO - Following reports of people being assaulted by police and soldiers enforcing the lockdown, Ximba isn't taking any chances with his children.
MPHIKISENI XIMBA – ALEXANDRA RESIDENT
XIMBA - They are not allowed to go outside, they must stay indoors.
CB – Aren't they a handful?
XIMBA – They are. They are restless because they are children and they want to play.
VO – A few streets from Ximba's home, when soldiers allegedly spotted Collins Khoza enjoying a beer in his yard on Good Friday, they accused him of breaking lockdown rules. It is reported that the soldiers then assaulted Collin so severely, he later died.
Defence minister Nosiviwe Mapisa-Nqakula sent her condolences to the family.
NOSIVIWE MAPISA-NQAKULA – DEFENCE AND MILITARY VETERANS MINISTER
We are saddened by what happened. The investigation is conducted by the South African Police Services, by the military police and also the military ombuds office. We are therefore unable to comment at this point. In such cases, obviously the law will take its course.
VO - Images of law enforcers ordering people to do press-ups, roll on the ground and other forms of punishment flooded social media, prompting human rights activist Mahlomola Ledwaba to team up with independent lawyers and represent victims against the state without charge.
MAHLOMOLA LEDWABA – HUMAN RIGHTS ACTIVIST
We received a lot of calls from the community about the soldiers and the police who are harassing them.
VO – He says the violent history between the army and township residents means many in these communities still fear security forces and are less likely to sue.
MAHLOMOLA LEDWABA – HUMAN RIGHTS ACTIVIST
The police and the soldiers are undermining us. Many people are scared to go to the police station and report the matters.
VO – Just seven days into lockdown and the Independent Police Investigative Directorate had its hands full, investigating 38 cases of police brutality --- including 8 deaths at the time.
The Defence Ministry, also ordered senior army officials to “deal with those members proven to have used excessive or unnecessary force.”
Meanwhile, Gauteng moved to establish its first screening and treatment facilities starting in Alexandra.
Premier David Makhura was there.
DAVID MAKHURA – GAUTENG PREMIER
More than 4 000 community health workers who are involved is intensive mass testing are spread throughout the five regions in our province.

VO - Many of those who live in Alexandra, work in neighbouring Sandton, where the highest number of infections in the province has been recorded.
WESTERN CAPE
VO – Khayelitsha in the Western Cape was the first township to record a case of Covid-19.
Axolile Notywala of the Social Justice Coalition says access to clean water remains a huge complaint for residents.
AXOLILE NOTYWALA – SOCIAL JUSTICE COALITION
Approximately 250 to 300 thousand people do not have access to basic or sufficient water.
VO – Earlier this year, residents were excited when water began gushing from this hole, possibly from a leaking underground pipe system. But they soon realised that it just wasn’t safe to drink.
LADIES CHATTING AT WATERING HOLE
- The first time I drank this water, I got diarrhea.
- We don't know where it comes from but this hole doesn't run dry.
VO – They also don't know whether the water is safe to use for their laundry so they still have to walk long distances to get drinking water.
Government has now identified communities where more than forty-one thousand water tanks are being installed.
KZN

VO – In KwaZulu Natal, physical distancing and self-isolation is out of the question for people like Thenjiswa Qeda from Lamontville.
THENJISWA QEDA – LAMONTVILLE RESIDENT
We moved here in 2010. Government moved us here from our shacks up the road and said we would live here for six months while they build our RDP houses. We are still here.
VO – She fears that if anyone in her family were to contract the virus, everyone inside the single-room home would be at risk.
THENJISWA QEDA – LAMONTVILLE RESIDENT
There's a lot of us in this house and there's nothing we can do about it.
VO - The lockdown has further illustrated the divide between the have's and the have-not's.
AXOLILE NOTYWALA – SOCIAL JUSTICE COALITION
Many people live on small pieces of land where there are no spaces to move. They don't have access to piped water within their homes. Think about having to collect 25 litres of water every day. People have to drink from this water, people have to cook from this water, people have to bath from this water, and now they have to wash their hands for twenty seconds, regularly.
LIMPOPO
VO – In Limpopo, it’s been a challenge maintaining a safe distance in long queues at food stores says freelance journalist Livhuwani Madadzhe.


LIVHUWANI MADADZHE – LIVHU ONLINE TV
Along the queue people are just standing close to each other, sneezing, coughing, touching each other.
VO – Sanitiser is a luxury many people cannot afford.
LIVHUWANI MADADZHE – LIVHU ONLINE TV
They tell us that: “We cannot choose sanitiser instead of buying a braai pack or meat.”
EASTERN CAPE
VO – On Sundays, townships are generally a hive of activity with worshipers heading to different churches.
But lockdown regulations prohibit gatherings and in the Eastern Cape, police arrested churchgoers who defy the rules.
To encourage social distancing, authorities resort to public service announcements on loudspeakers.
UPSOUND – GCIS EC FOOTAGE CREDIT
Can we please make sure that, in-between everyone in the queue, there is space?
VO – South Africa's prompt response to the pandemic helped decrease the number of new infections from 110 cases in the week before the lockdown to 67 in the second week of the lockdown.
But on Thursday, the country recorded fourteen deaths, the highest in a single day, and ninety-nine new infections – igniting the possibility of an even longer lockdown.
Interventions by NGO's and the private sector have been instrumental in supporting underprivileged communities.

LINK – For many feeling the lockdown pinch in the townships, charity organisations have come to the rescue by providing food parcels and soap for those who cannot afford sanitiser.
VO - More than anything, people in Alexandra need food, says philanthropist Linda Twala, whose organisation Twala Ama Afrika distributes food parcels in the township.
LINDA TWALA – TWALA AMA AFRIKA
We need the government to bring more food. Right now as we speak, there are people who have got no food in their houses.
VO – Salaamedia, a group of humanitarian journalists, began raising funds for soap long before the lockdown, says Journo Azhar Vadi.
AZHAR VADI - SALAAMEDIA
We know the poverty levels and just that tiny bar of soap is sometimes something that's so difficult to come by.
VO – Fatima Sookharia activated the #CoronaSoldiers initiative to collect protective gear for healthcare workers.
FATIMA SOOKHARIA - SALAAMEDIA
There's these guys who are so little, they are sixteen years old and they have reached out to us and they have said they are going to provide the Salaam foundation with these masks. so that we can assist.
VO - Experts warn that early termination of the lockdown could lead to a new surge in infections. Authorities will do weekly assessments of trends to plan for the weeks ahead.
LINK – Despite the challenges presented by the virus and the subsequent lockdown, the spirit of resilience among South Africans remains unbroken and even in these uncertain times, unity prevails and songs of hope reverberate.

AXOLILE NOTYWALA – SOCIAL JUSTICE COALITION
I think it's important for everyone to follow the instructions and the regulations that have been issued out by government.
MPHIKISENI XIMBA – ALEXANDRA RESIDENT
We listen because we want to be safe.

PROMOS

South Africa, an unequal society with a strained healthcare system and millions living in poverty – the spread of the Coronavirus exposes how vulnerable the majority of the country still is.

Government fears that it's in densely populated townships and informal settlements like Alexandra and Khayelitsha that the spread of the Coronavirus could be utterly devastating.

The World Health Organisation advises social distancing and regular handwashing to curb the spread of Covid-19 but how can this happen in SA's overpopulated informal settlements?

Think about having to collect 25 litres of water every day. People have to drink from this water, people have to cook from this water, people have to bath from this water, and now they have to wash their hands for twenty seconds, regularly. LIMPOPO VO – In Limpopo, it’s been a challenge maintaining a safe distance in long queues at food stores says freelance journalist Livhuwani Madadzhe. LIVHUWANI MADADZHE – LIVHU ONLINE TV Along the queue people are just standing close to each other, sneezing, coughing, touching each other. VO – Sanitiser is a luxury many people cannot afford. LIVHUWANI MADADZHE – LIVHU ONLINE TV They tell us that: “We cannot choose sanitiser instead of buying a braai pack or meat.” EASTERN CAPE VO – On Sundays, townships are generally a hive of activity with worshipers heading to different churches. But lockdown regulations prohibit gatherings and in the Eastern Cape, police arrested churchgoers who defy the rules. To encourage social distancing, authorities resort to public service announcements on loudspeakers. UPSOUND – GCIS EC FOOTAGE CREDIT Can we please make sure that, in-between everyone in the queue, there is space? VO – South Africa's prompt response to the pandemic helped decrease the number of new infections from 110 cases in the week before the lockdown to 67 in the second week of the lockdown. But on Thursday, the country recorded fourteen deaths, the highest in a single day, and ninety-nine new infections – igniting the possibility of an even longer lockdown. Interventions by NGO's and the private sector have been instrumental in supporting underprivileged communities. LINK – For many feeling the lockdown pinch in the townships, charity organisations have come to the rescue by providing food parcels and soap for those who cannot afford sanitiser. VO - More than anything, people in Alexandra need food, says philanthropist Linda Twala, whose organisation Twala Ama Afrika distributes food parcels in the township. LINDA TWALA – TWALA AMA AFRIKA We need the government to bring more food. Right now as we speak, there are people who have got no food in their houses. VO – Salaamedia, a group of humanitarian journalists, began raising funds for soap long before the lockdown, says Journo Azhar Vadi. AZHAR VADI - SALAAMEDIA We know the poverty levels and just that tiny bar of soap is sometimes something that's so difficult to come by. VO – Fatima Sookharia activated the #CoronaSoldiers initiative to collect protective gear for healthcare workers. FATIMA SOOKHARIA - SALAAMEDIA There's these guys who are so little, they are sixteen years old and they have reached out to us and they have said they are going to provide the Salaam foundation with these masks. so that we can assist. VO - Experts warn that early termination of the lockdown could lead to a new surge in infections. Authorities will do weekly assessments of trends to plan for the weeks ahead. LINK – Despite the challenges presented by the virus and the subsequent lockdown, the spirit of resilience among South Africans remains unbroken and even in these uncertain times, unity prevails and songs of hope reverberate. AXOLILE NOTYWALA – SOCIAL JUSTICE COALITION I think it's important for everyone to follow the instructions and the regulations that have been issued out by government. MPHIKISENI XIMBA – ALEXANDRA RESIDENT We listen because we want to be safe. PROMOS South Africa, an unequal society with a strained healthcare system and millions living in poverty – the spread of the Coronavirus exposes how vulnerable the majority of the country still is. Government fears that it's in densely populated townships and informal settlements like Alexandra and Khayelitsha that the spread of the Coronavirus could be utterly devastating. The World Health Organisation advises social distancing and regular handwashing to curb the spread of Covid-19 but how can this happen in SA's overpopulated informal settlements?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Accused of not taking the Covid-19 pandemic seriously, residents in townships and informal settlements say they are doing the best they can with the little they have.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Following the first confirmed case of Covid-19 in Alexandra, we speak to residents and organisations who say they are putting up a good fight but might lose due to population density in the area. We spend a day with Linda Twala, a beloved businessman and philanthropist in Alexandra who is known for being hands-on in his community outreach programs. We go from his charity storeroom where food parcels are prepared for distribution among the needy and elderly in Alexandra, and we see him making deliveries and interact with beneficiaries. We also get to interview the beneficiaries about what they are doing to protect themselves from the virus.
metadata.Summary: The challenges in informal settlements are well-known but organisations and individuals are making a difference despite huge and valid concerns about population density. We focus on efforts to contain the spread in Alexandra seeing as it is the most densely populated township in Johannesburg and has most recently confirmed its first case. The organisations we speak to seek to address the two biggest concerns where the virus is concerned in townships – washing hands and people having enough food to minimise the need to go out and potentially expose themselves and others to the virus. Our focus takes a national approach as we use social media videos from other provinces including the Eastern Cape and an interview with Social Juctice Coalition to give an overview of the sanitation challenges associated with densely populated communities across the country. For the KZN perspective, we have a freelance producer and cameraman who is familiar with townships around the Durban area and will be able to take us into an informal settlement home of a family living a small shack and interview them about their water and sanitation challenges as well as the difficulty in maintaining social distancing. They will also tell us if KZN government interventions have filtered to them and if they have been able to access social welfare assistance. We will use a graphic to separate the stories from each province so that they do not pile on top of each other.
metadata.Further information: We also cover Soweto where Salaamedia, an organisation of humanitarian journalists, started collecting soap donations as soon as news of the virus spread under the tag #SoapBarCampaign. Their beneficiaries are mainly homes for the disadvantaged in Soweto where many people share dorms and dining halls. Part of their #CoronaSoldiers campaign has been to educate their beneficiaries about the virus because it was apparent that information had not really filtered to people on the ground – many still don't understand how the virus affects the body and exactly why the lockdown is necessary. They also run a Facebook Live station with over 21 000 followers where they try to reach people on social media and give them up-to-date and accurate information on the virus. Among their priorities right now is sourcing face masks for health professionals as a response to widespread calls to protect the very healthcare workers who service generally underprivileged communities.
